pronunciation.approximation: FULL-ah — a short, rounded u as in 'put', a genuinely long, doubled l, and a short open 'ah'; two even syllables, stress on the first.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Fulla is a transparent formation on fullr, 'full' — the same word as English 'full' and German 'voll' — so the name means 'Fullness, Plenty', an abstract noun worn as a personal name, like her sister ásynjur Sjǫfn and Lofn. The double l is a true geminate, held twice as long as a single l. The normalized Old Norse form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth — so the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography, never about the goddess.

domains.title: The Keeper of the Casket
domains.subtitle: Abundance, Secrets — the Trusted One of Frigg's Hall
domains.lead: Fulla is Frigg's handmaid and confidante — the virgin goddess who goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head, who carries the queen's little box, looks after her shoes, and shares her secret counsels. Her name is Fullness itself: plenty made a person, trusted with everything a queen cannot carry alone.

cards.name: The Eski
cards.desc: Frigg's little casket, which Fulla carries — the portable treasury of the queen of the gods, and the clearest badge of her office.

cards.name: The Golden Band
cards.desc: The gold snood Fulla wears about her loose hair — Snorri's one detail of dress, and the mark of wealth her name promises.

cards.name: The Queen's Shoes
cards.desc: Fulla looks after Frigg's footwear — the humblest duty in the catalogue, and the surest sign of a servant admitted to every chamber.

cards.name: The Shared Counsels
cards.desc: She shares Frigg's leyniráðagørðir — the queen's secret deliberations: the duty that outranks every object she carries.

symbols.name: The eski (little casket)
symbols.meaning: Frigg's portable treasure-box, entrusted to the hand that never lets it go — custody as a form of intimacy

symbols.name: The golden hair-band
symbols.meaning: The virgin's loose hair bound with gold — unmarried freedom dressed in plenty

symbols.name: Frigg's shoes
symbols.meaning: The queen's footwear in her keeping — the lowest duty held by the highest confidence

symbols.name: The finger-ring from Hel
symbols.meaning: Nanna's gift carried back by Hermóðr — a token from the dead addressed, of all the ásynjur, to her

mythology.lead: Fulla has no saga of her own: her dossier is four precise notices, and every one of them places her at Frigg's side. What the tradition lost in narrative it kept in definition — no goddess in the Edda is more exactly described in a single sentence.

myths.title: The Keeper of the Casket
myths.text: Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur gives Fulla her entire portrait in one sentence, and the tradition never varies it: 'Fulla is a virgin and goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head; she carries Frigg's eski, looks after her footwear, and shares her secret counsels with her.' The three duties descend in rank and rise in intimacy — the box is treasure, the shoes are service, the counsels are trust itself. She is named immediately after Gná, Frigg's errand-rider, and the pairing has stuck: where Gná carries the queen's words out through the worlds, Fulla keeps the queen's words that never leave the hall. Scholars since Grimm have read both as hypostases of Frigg — aspects of the queen walking about as attendants — but the Edda keeps them as persons, and Fulla's golden band and loose hair make her the most visually fixed of all the minor ásynjur.

myths.title: The Warning to Geirröðr
myths.text: Fulla's one errand in the Poetic Edda is given in prose, at the head of Grímnismál. Óðinn and Frigg had quarrelled over their foster-sons: Frigg accused King Geirröðr, Óðinn's favourite, of being so stingy he tortured his guests for lack of food, and Óðinn laid a wager on his man and set off disguised to test him. Frigg, knowing the road, sent her handmaid Fulla to Geirröðr ahead of him, to warn the king to beware of a certain sorcerer coming to his land to bewitch him — and gave her the token by which he could be known: no dog, however fierce, would leap at him. The warning is the trap: Geirröðr seized the blue-cloaked stranger, named Grímnir, and tortured him between two fires — and out of that fire the god spoke the whole catalogue of the worlds. Fulla appears only to deliver the message and vanish, but the wager, the torture, and the poem's entire revelation turn on her errand.

myths.title: The Ring from Hel
myths.text: When Hermóðr rode nine nights to ransom Baldr and came home with the tidings, he brought tokens from the dead: Baldr sent back the ring Draupnir to Óðinn, and Nanna — Baldr's wife, who had died of grief on his pyre — sent gifts out of Hel to the two women of Frigg's hall: a linen headdress for Frigg, and a finger-ring for Fulla. It is the smallest bequest in the whole Baldr cycle, and the most telling: when a dead goddess thinks of Ásgarðr's household, she thinks of the queen and of the queen's handmaid by name. Fulla stands in that sentence exactly where her office puts her — the second woman of the hall, remembered with jewellery from beyond the world.

myths.title: Volla, Friia's Sister
myths.text: The one continental witness comes from a tenth-century Fulda manuscript, the Second Merseburg Charm — the only pagan theogonic text in Old High German. Phol and Wodan rode to the wood, and Balder's foal wrenched its foot; then the goddesses chant over it in sequence: Sinthgunt, Sunna her sister; Friia, Volla her sister; and at last Wodan, who knows how, and the limb is knit bone to bone and blood to blood. Since Jacob Grimm, Volla — Friia's sister — has widely been read as Fulla, Frigg's attendant: the name is the exact Old High German form of the same word, and the charm puts her, precisely as the Edda does, at Friia's right hand. The identification is argued, not proven, and the handbooks counsel the usual caution — but if it holds, Fulla is one of the very few Norse goddesses with a continental footprint older than the Icelandic books.

lore.syncretism: Fulla's cross-border life runs through one word and one relationship. The word is fullr: Proto-Germanic *fullaz gives English 'full', German 'voll', Gothic fulls, and Old Norse Fulla — a goddess whose name is the ordinary adjective turned abstract noun, 'Fullness'. The relationship is the one the Merseburg Charm preserves: Volla beside Friia, as Fulla beside Frigg — and since Grimm, the identification of the two has been the standing reading, with Simek registering both the fit and the doubt. The deeper syncretic question is what kind of being she is. Gylfaginning's ásynjur catalogue is full of abstract-noun goddesses — Sjǫfn ('affection'), Lofn ('praise, permission'), Vár ('vows') — and scholars have long suspected that Fulla, Gná, and their sisters are facets of Frigg herself, the queen's plenitude and far-ranging given names and errands of their own. Whether she began as an independent goddess of plenty or as an aspect that walked off on its own, the sources keep her a person: she receives a ring, runs an errand, and wears her own gold.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fulla's afterlife is scholarly and liturgical rather than popular. Grimm devoted a chapter of Teutonic Mythology to her and Volla, and every handbook since — Simek, Orchard, Lindow — keeps her as the standing example of the abstract-noun ásynja, the goddess whose name tells you exactly what she is. Her image — loose hair, golden band, the queen's casket on her arm — became the fixed Victorian and modern picture of the trusted northern handmaid, and she appears in nearly every retelling of the Baldr cycle by virtue of one finger-ring. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice keeps her at Frigg's side as a goddess of plenty, household trust, and well-kept secrets, invoked where abundance must be held in confidence. She never became a Marvel character or a video-game boss; she remained what the Edda made her — the most trusted person in the queen's hall, and the proof that in the northern pantheon even abundance has a keeper.
lore.extendedMeditation: Fulla is the goddess of what is held in trust. Every detail of her portrait is a form of custody: the casket she carries but does not own, the shoes she tends but does not wear, the counsels she shares but does not speak. Even her name works this way — Fullness is not a thing she does but a thing she keeps. The tradition gives her no adventure because her office is the adventure's opposite: Gná rides out with the queen's words; Fulla stays, and what is entrusted to her stays with her. Nanna's ring from Hel is the tradition's own verdict on that office — when the dead send gifts home, they send one to the keeper. In a mythology that ends in fire and betrayal, Fulla is the quiet counterweight: the proof that some things, once entrusted, are simply kept.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Fulla — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᚢᛚᛅ (f-u-l-a, the sixteen-rune row writing the geminate ll with a single ᛚ). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: fulla.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Fulla is an entirely textual goddess: no cult site, toponym, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the runic corpus is silent — unsurprising for a figure the sources place inside the queen's household rather than in the public cult. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The Grímnismál prose, which preserves her one errand, survives in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); her portrait in Gylfaginning 35 and her ring in Gylfaginning 49 come with the Prose Edda codices of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and her name recurs in the þulur, the metrical name-lists appended to Skáldskaparmál. The one continental witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, copied into a theological manuscript at Fulda in the tenth century and now in the Merseburg cathedral library: its Volla, sister of Friia, is the only attestation of the figure outside Iceland and, if the identification holds, the oldest by centuries.
